title: Repeating Efficiently
goals: Trace a loop by testing its condition before every repetition
Distinguish the number of repetitions from the final value and include zero repetitions
Explain why an update reaches a stopping condition or why a faulty loop keeps repeating
vocabulary: Instructions that repeat according to a stated rule
One execution of the repeated body
The instructions performed on each iteration
The situation in which repetition ends
A change that brings the state closer to a stopping condition

worked_example.title: Check starts that need no repetitions

blocks.text: While tests before the body. If the first test is false, the body runs zero times. Do not add 2 once just because a loop is present. Starting at 7 or 8 is a useful test of this rule.

A loop that stops when the counter is no longer below 7 does not promise to finish at exactly 7. Starting at 6 produces 8. Passing the boundary is allowed by these instructions. Always report the actual final state instead of replacing it with the threshold.

guided_practice.title: Check the first test
guided_practice.prompt: Use the same below 8 loop with add 2. Make separate runs from 8 and 9. Explain how many times the body runs and what each run reports. Why would adding 2 once be an error?
guided_practice.answer: Both first tests are false. Each run has zero iterations, reporting its unchanged starting value: 8 or 9. Adding 2 once would execute the body despite a false first test.

independent_case.title: Transfer to a countdown
independent_case.task: A paper countdown starts at 7. While remaining is above 1, subtract 2. When false, report and stop. Trace the run and count iterations. Repeat from 6 and from 1. Explain why the final value need not equal 1. What happens from 7 if subtract 2 is replaced by subtract 0?
independent_case.answer: From 7: 7 true, 5 true, 3 true, 1 false; three iterations, report 1. From 6: 6 true, 4 true, 2 true, 0 false; three iterations, report 0. From 1: first test false, zero iterations, report 1. Above 1 stops at 1 or below. Subtracting 0 from 7 leaves every test true, so that faulty run never reports.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: Every loop runs at least once
Point to the test before the body. From 7 under below 7 the first test is false, so no update is permitted.
The final value must equal the threshold
Trace start 6 under add 2 and below 7. The loop reports 8 because the stopping requirement is no longer below 7.
Tests and iterations are the same count
Count body executions separately and show the last false test with no body action.
A changing number guarantees a stop
Compare below 7 with not equal to 7 from 6 under add 2. Even numbers pass 7 without equalling it.

blocks.text: VISUAL MECHANISM
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.

Visual card for the process stage: run the loop body and update progress
Visual card for the output stage: finished pattern when the stop condition is met

blocks.text: INPUT  starting state and repeat count
PROCESS  run the loop body and update progress
OUTPUT  finished pattern when the stop condition is met
CORE IDEA  A loop repeats a useful step until a stopping condition is met.

UNDER THE HOOD  A loop requires an initialization, body, update, and termination condition. Repetition is safe only when each iteration moves state toward stopping; otherwise the loop may run forever or the wrong number of times.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
A closer explanation

blocks.title: A complete loop trace
blocks.caption: Read the rows from top to bottom as one run. Each true test performs one addition and returns to the test. The final false test performs no addition.

blocks.text: The trace has four tests but only three iterations. The false test is evidence that this run stops. A list ending at 5 would be incomplete, while a list continuing to 9 would include an addition the loop did not authorise.

Write the current value, the test result and the action on every row. Repeated values can matter: if the body does not change the state used by the test, the same true test may occur again. Do not erase these rows simply because they look unhelpful.
Connect the picture and the explanation
Point to the input, the deciding step and the result in this week’s visual. Explain the same step in ordinary words. A picture helps when you can say what each part represents.

Comparison picture for Stop too early: one item remains; off-by-one error

blocks.text: CASE 1 — Square  Clue: repeat move and turn 4 times. Meaning: counted loop.
CASE 2 — Pick cards  Clue: repeat until pile empty. Meaning: condition loop.
CASE 3 — No counter update  Clue: condition never changes. Meaning: infinite loop risk.
CASE 4 — Stop too early  Clue: one item remains. Meaning: off-by-one error.
BOUNDARY  Repeat forever is not an efficient algorithm unless endless operation is truly the goal and can be stopped safely.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
